intent: Let an agent confirm elements that only fix wording.

edit.summary:
I added a way for an agent to confirm elements that only fix wording. All edits are in `authoring/authoring.domain.yaml`, now version 13. I haven't compiled it or run its scenarios.

- **Role:** there is a new `agent` role, with one actor, `bot`, in the world.
- **Flag:** `Element` has an optional `wording_only` boolean. `propose_element` takes it as an optional param.
- **Action:** the new `confirm_wording_element` is open to the `agent` role. A precondition, `wording-only`, requires `target.wording_only == true`. It runs the same `confirm_element` call as the human action and replies with `record_confirmation`.
- **Transitions:** from `proposed`, the new action moves an element to `confirmed`. In `unknown` and `confirmed` it is `n/a`.
- **Scenario:** I added fixture `E4`, a wording-only element, and the scenario `an-agent-confirms-only-wording-fixes`. In it the agent is denied on `E1` (not flagged) and succeeds on `E4`.
- **Unchanged:** `confirm_element` and `confirm_all_proposed` still require a person.
- **Source status:** the new action and its transition cell are marked `status: proposed`, because no interview line backs them yet.

**Needs review:**
- The rule `only-a-person-element-confirmed` still says only a person brings an `Element` to `confirmed`. That now contradicts the new action. I left the rule alone because changing it is a policy decision, so the check may flag it.
- Nothing stops an agent from proposing an element and flagging it `wording_only` itself. Only the owner can call `propose_element` today, so I didn't add a guard.

findings.problem: The new action confirm_wording_element lets an agent bring an Element to confirmed, with no requires: human. The rule only-a-person-element-confirmed says only a person brings an Element to confirmed, and that every action doing so requires a person. The rule now contradicts the action and its Element matrix cell. It will block the action, or the action defeats the rule. The change neither amends nor exempts the rule.

Text that says only a person confirms is now false. The glossary says an element is 'confirmed only by a person', and confirm_element says 'Only a person confirms.' Element.description says 'proposed by an agent or confirmed by a person'. The purpose, the announcement and the rule reasons also rest on this guarantee. None were updated.

The wording_only flag is the only safeguard on an agent's confirmation, and nothing checks it. The proposer sets it freely on propose_element, and nothing ties it to the path or value actually being a wording change. A substantive element (an action, a rule, a precondition) can be flagged wording_only and then confirmed with no person seeing it. The agent also passes its own id as the approver, so the confirmation is recorded as the agent's approval of something that may not be wording.

The new action and its matrix cell are status: proposed and cite ADR-0037, an unrelated record, rather than the change request or an owner decision. A change that weakens the human-confirmation guarantee has no confirming source. It is also unclear whether a proposed action or cell is live once deployed. If it is live, an unconfirmed agent-confirmation path is running. If it is not, the scenario that exercises it will fail.

The first step of the scenario targets E1, which has no wording_only value. The check target.wording_only == true runs on an unset optional field, so the denial may come out as an evaluation error rather than denied_by: wording-only. The scenario also checks only the confirm and deny cases. It does not check that the agent cannot call confirm_element, and it does not check that an already confirmed or unknown wording element is refused.

The rule only-a-person-element-confirmed says only a person brings an Element to confirmed, and that confirm_element is the only action that does so. The new confirm_wording_element has an agent actor and no `requires: human`, and its matrix cell moves a proposed Element to confirmed. That contradicts the rule, and its reason text is now false. Either the rule has to be scoped or amended, or the action cannot exist as written.

Several statements still say a person is the only one who confirms. The confirm_element description says 'Only a person confirms.' The glossary entry for element says it is 'confirmed only by a person.' The Element object description says 'confirmed by a person.' Only the new action's own description acknowledges the exception.

The wording-only flag is self-declared. The owner sets `wording_only` when proposing the element, and the only check is `target.wording_only == true`. Nothing verifies that the element really only fixes wording, so a substantive element flagged wording-only can be confirmed by an agent with no person involved. This weakens the human-confirmation guarantee on the very elements the owner wants to review.

The new action calls the kernel's confirm_element with `approver: actor.id`, so an agent id (bot) is recorded as the approver of a confirmed element. The kernel and the working copy may expect a person as approver, and the deployed behaviour of that call for an agent is unverified. The record of who approved is also no longer necessarily a person.

The new action and its matrix cell are marked `status: proposed`, and the cell cites an ADR that predates this change instead of this request. The change is therefore unconfirmed and unsourced, yet it is deployed with version 13. The new matrix cell can also be dropped or flagged by the 'confirmed only' conventions used elsewhere.

The rule says only a person brings an Element to confirmed, and that every action that does so requires a person. The new confirm_wording_element action is performed by the agent role, has no `requires: human`, and its matrix cell moves an Element from proposed to confirmed. The rule is now false and contradicts the action. As written, either the rule blocks the new action or the action silently bypasses the rule.

The glossary entry for 'element' still says elements are drafted by an agent and 'confirmed only by a person'. The Element object description likewise says 'confirmed by a person', and confirm_element says 'Only a person confirms'. The change makes these statements untrue, since an agent can now confirm wording-only elements.

The wording_only flag is set by whoever proposes the element, through a free parameter on propose_element, and nothing checks that the element really only fixes wording. The precondition just trusts the flag. A proposer can mark a substantive element wording_only and have an agent confirm it with no person involved. That defeats the stated aim of keeping substance for the owner's attention.

confirm_wording_element calls the kernel's confirm_element with approver set to the agent's id. The kernel's confirmation and approval path (the human-only confirm_element, the 'confirmed only by a person' glossary) assumes a human approver. The kernel may refuse the call, or the agent will be recorded as the approver of a confirmed element. The domain does not say how this is handled.

The new action and its matrix cell are marked `status: proposed`, and their source is the ADR-0037 record. That record is a generic citation about the self-domains switch and does not support agents confirming elements. The change is unconfirmed by a person, yet it grants the agent role new authority. Deploying it would put an unconfirmed rule into the live domain.

The rule only-a-person-element-confirmed says only a person brings an Element to confirmed, and that confirm_element is the only action that does so. The new confirm_wording_element has an agent actor, no `requires: human`, and a matrix cell moving Element from proposed to confirmed. It contradicts the rule, and the rule's reason text is now false. The rule was not changed, so either the action is denied or the rule is not enforced.

The glossary entry for 'element' still says an element is 'confirmed only by a person'. The description of confirm_element also says 'Only a person confirms.' Both are now untrue, because an agent can confirm wording-only elements.

Whether an element counts as wording-only is a flag that the proposer sets with `wording_only` on propose_element. Nothing checks that the element really only fixes wording. Anyone who proposes an element can set the flag on a substantive one, and an agent can then confirm it with no person involved. That defeats the human-confirmation guarantee the change is meant to keep for non-wording elements. The flag is also not passed to the kernel's propose_element call, so the kernel cannot see it.

confirm_wording_element passes `approver: actor.id` to the kernel's confirm_element call, so the agent's id ('bot') is recorded as the approver of the element. Anything that reads that approver as a person's approval, such as the audit trail or the deploy floor, would now see a non-person approver.

The new action and its matrix cell are marked `status: proposed`, yet they ship in version 13. They have not been confirmed by a person, which is the review rule this domain applies to its own elements. In this very change an unconfirmed element is what grants the agent confirmation power.

The scenario starts `from_world: E4` but its first step targets E1. E1 is not linked to E4, so it may not be loaded into the scenario's state. The denied_by: wording-only check may then fail on a missing target instead of testing the precondition.

Rule only-a-person-element-confirmed says only a person brings an Element to confirmed, and that confirm_element is the only action that does so. The new confirm_wording_element has an agent bring an Element to confirmed (matrix proposed -> confirmed) without requires: human. The rule and the new action directly contradict each other. Either the rule denies the action at deploy or the rule is silently weakened, and its reason text is now false.

Text elsewhere still says only a person confirms an element. The glossary entry 'element' says 'confirmed only by a person'. The confirm_element description says 'Only a person confirms'. The Element object description says 'proposed by an agent or confirmed by a person'. The change leaves all three stale.

The wording_only flag is set by whoever proposes the element, through the optional propose_element param, and nothing checks that the element really only fixes wording. Anyone who proposes can mark a substantive element wording_only and an agent can then confirm it, bypassing the human-confirmation safeguard. The flag is also not passed in the propose_element kernel call, so the working copy never learns of it, and the claim of low risk is unenforced.
